speaker: Noam Brown
title: Really Big Test-Time Compute in AI with OpenAI's Noam Brown
question: In frontier AI, why doesn't giving a reasoning model an arbitrarily large inference budget make it superintelligent across all tasks?
guest: First of all, there are some benchmarks where models just will not improve with more inference budget. Factual retrieval questions fall into this category: if you ask someone when Abraham Lincoln was born and they don't know, sitting there thinking for a week without Wikipedia won't help them do better than thinking for five seconds. Same with models—a little thinking helps, but a week won't suddenly make them remember dates. On the other extreme, there are benchmarks where models obviously keep improving without limit, like Sudoku. You can try random numbers, check if they match all the constraints, and with enough time solve any puzzle. All benchmarks exist somewhere between these two extremes. Models aren't at the level where enough test-time compute lets them do all of our jobs because there are things where they simply won't improve. For research in particular, they don't have very good research taste right now. They're a very good complement to researchers, and I'm much more effective using them, but they're not able to fully replace the whole research cycle just with more test-time compute.

points.core: Unbounded test-time compute scaling primarily works on tasks with verifiable search spaces.
points.note: Accept: constraint-checkable problems like Sudoku, math proofs, or formal verification where trial-and-check guarantees progress. Do not credit: vague statements that some tasks are harder than others.

points.core: Extra thinking time cannot recover missing factual knowledge without external information retrieval.
points.note: Accept: pure recall questions plateau quickly because thinking for a week cannot surface an unknown fact without tools or lookup. Do not credit: general complaints about hallucinations.

points.core: Current reasoning models still lack the research taste needed for open-ended discovery.
points.note: Accept: lacking judgment on which novel directions or hypotheses to pursue, making them complements rather than full replacements for researchers. Do not credit: generic claims that AI lacks human creativity or consciousness.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because extra inference compute amplifies what a model already knows and can do; it doesn't supply what's missing. More thinking time lets a model search more candidate solutions, check its work, and break problems into steps, but the returns are bounded by several things.

First, the search is only as good as the model's learned priors and its ability to recognise a correct answer. On tasks without a cheap verifier (novel research, strategy, judgment calls), sampling more just produces more plausible-looking candidates it can't reliably rank.

Second, errors compound over long reasoning chains. Small per-step mistakes, drift from the goal, and limited context or memory mean very long deliberations often degrade rather than improve, so gains typically scale roughly logarithmically with compute and then plateau.

Third, many tasks are bottlenecked by things thought can't generate: missing knowledge, real-world data, experiments, and feedback from the environment.

Finally, a model can't reason its way to concepts or skills its training never gave it; that requires better training, not longer inference. Inference compute and training capability are complements, not substitutes.

points.why: The response explains how weak verification limits search but never establishes that a verifiable search space enables trial and check to keep making progress.
The response identifies missing knowledge as an information bottleneck that extra deliberation alone cannot overcome.
quotes: many tasks are bottlenecked by things thought can't generate: missing knowledge, real-world data, experiments, and feedback from the environment.

points.why: The response discusses difficulty ranking candidate answers without a verifier but leaves out the judgment needed to choose which research questions or hypotheses are worth pursuing.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Scaling inference compute lets a reasoning model search deeper, backtrack, and refine candidates, but its gains are bounded by verification, empirical knowledge, and the base model's representations. Test-time compute thrives in mathematics and coding because candidate solutions are easy to check; without a reliable verifier, as in open-ended strategy, creative work, or ambiguous real-world judgment, extra deliberation lacks a ground-truth signal to select better paths and often amplifies biases or self-rationalization.

Furthermore, deduction cannot replace missing information. Thinking longer extrapolates from existing weights and context, but pure contemplation cannot conjure unrecorded facts or substitute for active experimentation in the physical world. Even on purely abstract problems, inference-time search remains bottlenecked by architecture and priors: when a required conceptual leap lies far outside learned abstractions, the model's own flawed heuristics steer search into dead ends, while finite context windows and attention dilution cause ultra-long chains of thought to compound early framing errors and overthink rather than converge on truth.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
A bigger thinking budget mostly helps a model search more thoroughly through what it already knows how to do. It doesn't give the model new knowledge or new skills. Studies of RL-trained reasoners suggest training mostly brings out reasoning paths the base model could already produce: with enough attempts, the base model often matches them. If the right idea or fact isn't in the model at all, more tokens won't conjure it.

Gains from extra compute also flatten out. Accuracy tends to rise roughly with the logarithm of compute and then plateau. Long chains pile up small errors, overflow the usable context, and sometimes get worse with more thinking (so-called inverse scaling, or "overthinking").

Search is also only as good as the ability to check answers. In math or code, a model can test its candidates. In open-ended areas like strategy, science taste or writing, there's no reliable check, so sampling more just repeats the model's biases or games an imperfect reward signal. Finally, many tasks need information from outside the model, such as experiments, current data or physical feedback, which internal thinking can't replace.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: Scaling inference compute lets a reasoning model explore more solution paths, check its work, and refine answers, which yields major gains on verifiable problems like math or coding. However, an arbitrarily large test-time budget hits several fundamental ceilings. First, extra thinking only helps when the model can reliably tell better reasoning from worse; on open-ended, ambiguous, or hard-to-verify tasks, flawed self-evaluation causes it to overthink, loop, or rationalize errors rather than converge on truth. Second, test-time search only amplifies what already lies within the base model’s learned representations and priors—it cannot reliably generate missing world knowledge, new abstractions, or insights that sit outside its training distribution. Third, long reasoning traces face diminishing returns, context degradation, and compounding mistakes. Finally, many real-world problems cannot be solved by pure internal deliberation at all; they require external experimentation, empirical feedback, and interaction with the environment to uncover new information.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A larger inference budget gives a reasoning model more chances to work through a problem, explore alternatives, and check its answers. How much that helps depends on whether the model can find promising candidates and tell when it has found a good one. If it keeps making the same mistaken assumption, more reasoning can reinforce the error.

For some tasks, a reliable checker makes extra compute especially powerful. A model could, in principle, enumerate candidate proofs until it finds a valid one, if one exists. Many tasks lack that kind of feedback. A model trying to diagnose a machine may need a sensor reading it cannot obtain, and a model predicting an experiment may need evidence that only the experiment can supply. Some precisely defined problems are even undecidable in general.

So there’s no single ceiling that applies to every task. Extra compute can yield major gains where search and verification work, while missing information, unreliable feedback, and limits of computability can remain decisive regardless of the budget.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
More inference compute helps when a model can use it to explore alternatives, check its work, and recognize a better answer. In math, for example, extra attempts can pay off if the model can verify a proposed solution. But if it keeps making the same faulty assumption, it may spend a much larger budget producing variations of the same mistake.

Some limits go beyond reasoning skill. If two situations fit everything the model knows but require different actions, thinking longer cannot tell it which situation it faces. It needs an observation or feedback. And even when a solution is verifiable, finding it by search can take longer than the task allows.

An inference budget buys more computation. How much that improves performance depends on the model’s learned strategies, the information it can access, and whether it can tell when it has made progress.
